name: Senegalese Chicken Mafe (Peanut Stew)
writer_notes: SELECTOR: Page verified: full recipe, 5 servings, 519 cal / 30g protein per serving before rice. Peanut-butter thickened braise scales cleanly to 14 servings in one pot and portions by weight over rice. Every signature ingredient (peanut-butter, sweet-potatoes, crushed-tomatoes) is a live board commodity. No live chicken recipe uses a West African groundnut base (Jollof and Doro Wat are the only African chicken entries). Confidence: high, nutrition read directly from the recipe card. | HARVEST: Source lets the cook choose beef or chicken; use chicken for this run.
OVERRIDE Beef Chuck Roast: TITLE-PROTEIN SWAP: titled chicken; stew chunks -> chicken thigh (braise-stable cut), grams kept
intro_html: Mafe is Senegal's groundnut stew, and it has been feeding large tables on small budgets for a very long time. Peanut butter melts into tomato and broth until the whole pot turns the color of terra cotta and thickens on its own, no flour and no cream involved. Chicken goes in early and comes out falling apart. Over rice, each bowl runs {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein for about ${{cost_ps}} (at everyday cost). Peanut butter as a dinner ingredient is one of the best deals in the store and almost nobody uses it that way.
ingredients_display: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh (Member's Mark): 4.25 lb (1890 g)
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh, 4.25 lb: ~$13.42. Buy 5 lbs: $16.10.
Peanut Butter, 0.75 cups: ~$0.57. Buy 1 (covers about three batches).
Chicken Broth, 2.3 cartons: ~$3.28. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 3 32oz cartons.
Rice, 4 cups dry: ~$0.88. Buy 1 (covers this batch with some left over).
Pantry seasonings (smoked paprika, black pepper, salt): ~$0.74. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $25.16 across 14 servings, so roughly $1.80 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $30.31 across 14 servings, roughly $2.16 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $9.37 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $39.68. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a bowl (at everyday cost) for a West African stew that gets richer as it sits in the fridge. Chicken and canned tomatoes are the only lines worth watching, and a little peanut butter does the work a pint of cream would do in a European braise.
shop_smart: Buy the big jar of plain peanut butter and skip anything labeled natural or no-stir if you are counting pennies. This recipe uses less than a cup, so one jar covers several batches and the rest goes on toast.

Canned diced tomatoes are the volume in this pot and they are one of the few groceries that barely moved in price. Buy them by the case when they hit a sale, since they sit on a shelf for a year without complaining.
Boneless skinless thighs are the braising cut. They cost less per pound than breast and they will not turn stringy after an hour in a hot pot.
One jalapeno is the entire heat budget. Traditional mafe uses a scotch bonnet, so if your store carries habanero and you like the fire, one of those swaps in without changing the price much.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.

Season the chicken thighs with salt, black pepper and smoked paprika. Heat the vegetable oil in your largest pot over medium-high and brown the chicken in batches, working in a single layer so it colors instead of steams. Set it aside.
Drop the diced onion into the same pot and cook 5 to 6 minutes until soft and starting to catch, then add the garlic and the minced jalapeno and cook one more minute.
Stir the peanut butter directly into the hot onions and let it toast for a minute. It will look wrong and seize up. That is exactly what it should do.
Add the diced tomatoes and the chicken broth a little at a time, whisking as you go so the peanut butter loosens into a smooth sauce instead of clumping.

Return the chicken and any juices to the pot, bring it to a simmer, then cover and hold it at a low bubble for 45 minutes to an hour, stirring now and then so the bottom does not scorch. Peanut butter sauces catch fast.
While it simmers, cook the rice and let it steam covered off the heat for 10 minutes.
Pull the chicken, shred or chop it, and stir it back into the sauce with the cooked rice folded through so every bowl gets both.
portion_html: Set the pot on the scale, subtract the empty-pot weight, and divide by 14. Scoop the same number into all fourteen containers. Each one delivers {{cal}} calories, and this one genuinely tastes better on day three than it did on day one.

recipeIngredient: Boneless Skinless Chicken Thigh, 4.25 lb (1890 g)
steps: Season and brown the chicken thighs in oil in batches, then set aside.
Soften the onion, garlic and jalapeno in the same pot, then toast the peanut butter in with them.
Whisk in the diced tomatoes and broth gradually until the sauce is smooth.
Return the chicken, cover, and simmer 45 minutes to an hour, stirring so the bottom does not scorch.
Cook the rice, shred the chicken back into the sauce, fold in the rice, and portion into 14 containers.
